the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the issue of multilingualism, particularly in an enlarged europe, is now more important than ever. it is essential that european citizens have the necessary knowledge and skills to enable effective communication and facilitate mutual understanding. learning just one lingua franca is not enough. it is not, however, a reflection of european identity. the commission proposal follows up the decision of the european council in barcelona in march 2002, where the heads of state or government called for improving the acquisition of basic skills by teaching at an early age at least two foreign languages. they also called for the introduction of a common language proficiency index, in other words, a language test which would objectively measure citizens' knowledge of foreign languages. three years later, the commission proposes the creation of a european language proficiency index, common to all member states, with a high level of accuracy and reliability. the aim of the index will be to measure the proficiency of european citizens in foreign languages in four language skills: reading, comprehension, speaking and writing. the index will record language proficiency at each of the 6 levels of the common european framework of reference for languages of the council of europe. this common european reference framework is widely accepted and is already in use in many of the member states. i agree with the commission that the test of language proficiency should be carried out in the five most widely taught languages of the european union at an early stage. the inclusion of polish as a sixth language in the first phase will be decided by the budget, if that is possible. a eurobarometer survey published this week shows that english, with 38%, french with 14%, german also with 14%, spanish with 6% and italian with 3% are the 5 most popular languages in the european union chosen as foreign languages by european citizens however, i stress in the report that it is important at a later stage to extend this test to a wider range of languages of the european union. i would like to point out that non-community, minority and regional languages are not covered by this index. but they can be integrated into the strategy for multilingualism, on which the european parliament is preparing a report, and to which they are more suited in terms of content. i therefore do not agree with amendments nos 1 and 2, since they do not concern this report, do not contribute to the coherence of the text and do not correspond to the objectives of the language skills index. the language proficiency index is a technical instrument to be funded under an existing programme, namely the 'lifelong learning' programme, whose main objective is to substantially increase the mobility of citizens, workers or students in the european union. it is also worth noting that, according to recent data, although the proportion of primary school pupils learning a foreign language is increasing, the number of languages to be learned is unfortunately decreasing. in many countries, learning a foreign language tends to mean only learning english. the index can also be used to draw policy conclusions at european and national level. despite the commission's involvement in the process, member states should be actively involved in the implementation and development of the index, as they are the only ones who can provide further information on various factors affecting language proficiency, such as television, family environment, number of teaching hours, teaching experience and others. in general, the european language proficiency index is seen as a very important tool for collecting reliable data on the language skills of europeans, especially young people. it will also allow for comparison of language policies between member states, facilitating the identification and exchange of good practice to give a new impetus to such language teaching. mr president, commissioner, the knowledge of at least two foreign languages must be part of the basic skills and a representative element of the identity of european citizens living, studying, working and, in general, moving around the european union. let us not forget that 2006 is the 'european year of mobility', so i think it provides us with a very important opportunity to highlight the importance of the skills of european citizens and to provide young people with an incentive to give greater importance and attention to learning foreign languages. we look forward with great interest to the council's decisions on the language proficiency index on 18 may. i hope that the council will respond positively and understand its obligation to take account of the parameters and the evaluation of the european parliament's overall effort. in conclusion, i cannot help but mention the living example of multilingualism and its importance in this room: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a good one, but it is not enough to say that the directive is a good one.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, honourable members, thank you all for your contributions as well as your criticism. i think it will help in the ongoing discussion. when i entered politics many years ago, i learnt that there were three basic tasks for any political party or organisation. the first: to be able to describe reality, so that people will recognise reality as it is and agree that is the correct way to describe the world in which they live. the second task is to be able to put forward a vision, to say ‘this is where we want to go, that is what we want to achieve one day’. and, thirdly, to be able to change reality, to implement or enforce the changes that we want to achieve. i think that is still valid. it is exactly the commission’s line. we have a plan. we are willing to show leadership, first of all by being able to describe the reality we live in. indeed, we have tried to help by describing what we have heard through our plan d activities and from the member states and all the institutions involved in these activities, including visits to pubs. i was in london last friday to listen to the fears the british people expressed about the european union. secondly, we have been repeating that we want solidarity, prosperity and security, the values that we have set out in our treaties. thirdly, we have been showing the way, by changing the reality of the world in which we live. that is the way to engage people and to prove the added value of the european union: by working together to change people’s everyday lives. this we know from the eurobarometer surveys and from all our contacts. that is what people expect from us. that is how we can come back and approach the constitutional issues, because that is the way to prove that we have to change the way we take decisions. we must prove that we have to make the european union more open and democratic. we cannot stop that work now and say that we will just wait for a constitution. we have to do both things. we have to move in parallel on both those tracks. that is the only way to regain citizens’ trust. i feel a lot of frustration, as you do, at having lost a project of the kind the constitution represents. but the way to remedy that is not through personal attacks or attempts to engage only in bold rhetoric. there has been a lack of concrete suggestions as to what to do in france and the netherlands, where we have had a ‘no’ and where we have to engage with citizens again to regain their trust in any constitutional project. that is really what we ought to discuss. what kind of agenda can we establish to rebuild trust in those countries that are experiencing many problems? one idea was mentioned has my strong support. mr méndez de vigo suggested looking at the costs of a non-europe. i think that is an excellent idea and worth exploring. let us see if we can do that together and subsequently describe our findings. we have a number of examples to describe to people the costs of non-europe: energy policy and the fact that we do not have a foreign affairs minister, etc. it will make us less effective, less visible, less democratic and less open. we definitely have to end the blame game, because we are not alone in this: we need the member state governments. why should the swedish government, or any other government that has not yet ratified, engage in a project or stick their necks out in a situation where they see that there is no solution? nobody has presented a solution so far, but there are at least seven or eight different ideas on how to take this project forward. the commission’s idea is, therefore, to begin by proving the added value of the european project by changing reality and doing our best to respond to citizens’ concerns. whether it is energy policy, tackling unemployment or fighting crime and terrorism, we have to take action. meanwhile, we should also point out that a constitutional settlement would help us greatly to act even more effectively. at the same time, we must engage with governments to ensure that we sign up to the things we want to see realised in the future and that we share the same values and ideas for the future. that is a step towards finding a constitutional settlement. we do not want a two-speed europe or core groups. we believe that member states should act in unison and that we should hold the european project together. this means moving on both these tracks at the same time. we have demonstrated here that we have heard what people have told us regarding the priorities, and i think you agree with me. the first issues people raise when we speak to them in pubs, universities or elsewhere are the tangible issues. they want policies to be settled; they want us to take action on things that affect their everyday lives. that is what they expect from us. this also makes it easier to return to the constitutional issues. we can definitely follow up the idea of describing the costs of non-europe. we should also establish a timetable for a constitutional settlement. that is why we pointed to the opportunity next year, when we celebrate the 50th anniversary of the treaty of rome, for member states to agree on the way forward. this is our response to citizens’ concerns. being able to explain a citizens’ agenda – the people’s priorities – is a step forward. mr kirkhope is not here, but let me say that the fight against terrorism is a very important argument. are we really convinced that national vetoes should remain? the european evidence warrant is one example, and it is still blocked in the council. this is a very important proposal that would help our law-enforcement authorities to do their work more effectively. we will move forward with these proposals. the constitution is not dead. the estonians explained that they ratified it, not because they think that this issue will be solved immediately, but as a political statement. that was their purpose. however, they also realise that we have to look for solutions that satisfy both the french and the dutch people and the other member states, including those who said ‘yes’. it is not that easy to tell those countries that they have to do it again because we have made some changes. today we see no immediate solutions to this problem, but we will continue to show leadership on the constitutional issues as well as changing people’s reality and will set a policy agenda, a citizens’ agenda. the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i present to you today the proposal for a regulation on the marco polo ii programme. this regulation follows on from marco polo i, adopted in 2003, with the same objectives. the new programme, like the old one, aims to reduce congestion on the road network, improve the environmental performance of the transport system, and strengthen intermodal transport to help build an efficient and sustainable transport system. the programme runs from 1 january 2007 to 31 december 2013. the project will have a budget of €400 million, which is more than that of marco polo i. the structure of this programme is based on the granting of direct subsidies to airlines for the launch of intermodal services. it is the most efficient way of securing public funding. this programme was designed in the impact study so that one euro of grant for marco polo ii generates more than €6 in social and environmental benefits for society. while building on the mechanisms of the current programme, the regulation provides for two new types of action: those aimed at motorways of the sea and those aimed at traffic avoidance. these actions should help to reduce the volume of international road freight to meet a very high expectation of our citizens. the marco polo ii programme incorporates the concept of motorways of the sea, which was introduced in the transeuropean networks. it proposes appropriate targets for services linked to these motorways of the sea. calls for proposals are under way between germany and finland and between france and spain. actions under motorways of the sea are intended to limit road traffic in a given corridor. this clearly visible community added value benefits the european citizen and as such deserves a community contribution based on projects developed by consortia of shippers, transport operators and infrastructure providers. it is time to include the manufacturing and logistics sector more actively in a coherent strategy for sustainable development. that is why the commission has also planned measures to prevent trafficking. industry has already taken up this problem to streamline its supply chains and reduce distribution and transport costs. thus, there is a compatibility of interests between measures to increase the efficiency of industry and the political will to reduce the negative effects of transport by simply avoiding it. marco polo ii also extends the scope of the programme to all the european union's neighbours. today europe, and not just the union of 25 member states, will be at the forefront of an integrated transport market. our eastern neighbours, russia, belarus, ukraine, the balkans and the mediterranean region, form part of a large integrated market for transport services. production and supply chain characteristics do not stop at the borders of the eu-25. the council reached a partial general approach on 21 april 2005. i am glad that the rapporteur and the committee on transport of this parliament have sought to reach agreement at first reading. this constructive approach adopted by the two institutions should make it possible to adopt the regulation rapidly and launch the first call for tenders under marco polo ii. i thank you, mr rack, and the committee on transport and tourism which you chair. the compromise reached calls for four points: support for small and medium-sized enterprises, the thresholds for financing the various measures, the possible impact of measures to avoid traffic and special attention to sensitive and metropolitan areas. parliament has rightly pointed out the difficulties faced by small and mediumsized enterprises in accessing this programme. the new text will make it easier for them to do just that. i thank mr rack for making this point. the minimum funding thresholds for the various types of action have been reduced compared with those proposed by the commission. and the commission will be considering how to deal with the resulting increase in evaluation and monitoring work. the fear of a potential negative effect of anti-trafficking measures on employment and cohesion in certain regions has, i believe, been satisfactorily addressed. the new regulation also pays greater attention to sensitive and metropolitan areas. i would like to conclude, mr president, by apologizing for the length of the explanation of this proposal. i am again pleased that parliament has taken a very constructive approach to this report, which i believe has now resulted in a satisfactory text. i thank you and i thank in particular the rapporteur and the committee on transport and tourism.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr cashman, for a clear and useful report. his story about the cemetery keeper reminds me of a university rector who compared his job to being a cemetery keeper. he said: ‘i have a lot of people under me and nobody listening.’ the petitions offer a kaleidoscopic view of the concerns of many citizens today. they cover a wide range of policy areas, they cover practically all the member states and they cover a broad cross-section of civil society, from the individual citizen right up to the multinational ngos. your rapporteur is right to underline the importance of all the work represented by the thousand or more petitions you receive every year. there is no doubt that the committee on petitions offers citizens an important conduit for their feedback on european acts and policies. it thus contributes to a strengthening of democratic control over community legislation and its implementation at eu, national, regional and local level. i should like to pick up on three aspects in the report and resolution. the rapporteur was very kind and forthcoming towards the commission, so i do not want to raise any conflicts here. much is made in the report of the coexistence of the petitions procedure on the one hand and, on the other hand, the commission’s complaints procedures, sometimes leading to infringement proceedings. where there is coexistence, or even overlap, it is natural to make comparisons. i think that we should avoid getting into a discussion about the relative merits of petitions and complaints procedures. each procedure has its own legal basis and its own specificity and i believe that each of our institutions does well to preserve that, while respecting the needs of the other. in simple language, both procedures ultimately serve to ensure that eu law is applied to the benefit of the citizens. however, infringements are about the commission and the member state. the petitions procedure concerns the individual and their parliament. so each procedure is different in nature. that is not to say that we will not continue to strive for even better cooperation: the commission remains, as always, at the disposal of the committee. that brings me to the second point. as you know, the commission has already agreed to devote more attention to petitions concerning infringement proceedings in its annual report on the application of community law. it is, furthermore, important to remember that the amount of information given to the committee on petitions already exceeds that which is required by our interinstitutional agreement. this is important for transparency. the motion for a resolution argues that the commission does not act with sufficient speed and vigour in some cases where a petition and an infringement procedure are running in parallel. it therefore suggests that these procedures need to be better coordinated. let me just say one thing about that. it is only natural that the petitioner with a grievance may be in need of urgent redress, but let us remember that the ideal timescale of the individual petition will almost inevitably be shorter than the timescale of an infringement proceeding, which by definition takes a certain amount of time. we have, amongst other things, a duty of collaboration with the member states, which necessarily implies a multi-stage process. let us avoid raising unrealistic hopes in cases of overlapping. for the individual citizen, the successful outcome of an infringement procedure is not necessarily and automatically the ultimate and only thing to aim for. a successful outcome to an infringement procedure might not even directly entail the precise redress that the petitioner is seeking. we have several examples of that. the petitions procedure and the infringement procedure have different and distinct objectives, functions and roles. thus the efficiency of the commission’s complaints process cannot be formally linked to petitions. instead, let each of us, the commission and parliament, aim to ensure that our respective procedures – petitions and infringements – are fit for their respective purposes and let us continue our fruitful cooperation and strengthen that as much as possible. i shall refrain from commenting on some other details relating to processes and procedures. let me conclude by signalling my openness to the general message of this report: that petitions are important for democracy and for citizens. the commission is prepared to do as much as possible to improve our cooperation. (applause)

vice-president of the commission. mr president, first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr varvitsiotis. i welcome this initiative from austria, finland and sweden, which aims to apply the principle of mutual recognition to judgments in criminal matters imposing custodial sentences or measures involving the privation of liberty, for the purpose of their enforcement in the european union. the initiative will facilitate the social rehabilitation of offenders. it should in fact allow for rehabilitation measures to be taken in the state of nationality or permanent legal residence. one of the most controversial issues to arise in the discussion of this proposal in parliament and the council is the issue of the consent of the offender. i generally agree with your view and that of the rapporteur. more precisely, i consider that consent is not necessary for transfer to a member state to which the sentenced person is to be deported or transfer to the member state of residence of the sentenced person. however, consent should be necessary for the transfer to the member state of nationality of the sentenced person if that member state is not the member state of residence of the sentenced person. finally, i fully subscribe to your amendment aimed at adding a provision that the victims of the crime shall also be informed. the commission also considers it necessary that victims be informed, but only at their request, of the transfer of a sentenced person, because in this scenario the enforcement of any claims for damages becomes more complicated. i once again thank the rapporteur and can assure you that i will support most of your amendments during the discussions in the council.
the rapporteur. mr president, the subject we are discussing tonight is not new. it was first established by the council of europe convention of march 1983, which has been ratified by all the member states. the convention provided that convicted persons could be transferred to serve the remainder of their sentence only in their state of nationality and only with their consent and the consent of the states concerned. however, because of these bureaucratic formalities, this system did not work, so an additional protocol was needed on 18 december 1997, which did not require the consent of the convicted person. the protocol has not been signed by all the member states. this is how the initiative of austria, finland and sweden was born, which aims to speed up the procedure in the member state of origin or of permanent residence. the transfer of prisoners to serve their sentences is intended primarily to facilitate their life in prison and their easier reintegration into society after their release, since it is reasonable that a prisoner in the prison of the country of which he is a national will be able to communicate more easily with other prisoners, will be able to speak his language and not only that; in addition, he will be able to attend vocational training programmes which will help him to reintegrate smoothly into society and will also make it much easier for him to get in touch with his family or friends. the support of his family will be an important element for him. the simplification of procedures, so that the transfer of convicted persons is more flexible and less bureaucratic, was our main objective. i believe that what has been achieved is to better define the transfer criteria, to strengthen the principle of non bis in idem and the principle of specialisation and also to support the rights of victims, who should be informed about the whole process, including the transfer order of the convicted person. i agree with the commissioner that victims should only be informed if they so request, but in order for victims to know this, they must first be informed that there is such a procedure in progress. the member states' proposal covers only 32 serious offences and is based on a procedure for converting penalties into another penalty compatible with the law of the executing state. these positions, as voted unanimously by the committee on civil liberties, simplify and make more flexible the proposal of austria, finland and sweden, which provided for the granting of a permit to the member states through which the convicted person would pass on the presentation of multiple supporting documents. we have also amended the time limits set at each stage of the procedure to make them more realistic and at the same time to ensure a significant period of time spent in the executing state, so that the reintegration process is more complete and more effective. we have also settled the issues of amnesty and pardon, which are decided after consultation with the issuing and executing states. i think this proposal is another important step towards the convergence of criminal law in the member states of the european union. a great goal, but one that we must keep in mind, so that we can eventually unify criminal law. finally, mr president, i should like to thank the shadow rapporteurs of the other political groups and all those who tabled amendments for their excellent cooperation. i think the committee on civil liberties has taken a big step towards the unification of criminal law with this proposal.

the commission is very pleased with the report’s recognition that price- fixing liner conferences are no longer justified in today’s market conditions, either legally or economically. the thrust of our proposal is to increase eu competitiveness, much in keeping with the lisbon agenda. roughly 18% of imports and 21% of eu exports are affected by carriers’ ability to fix prices jointly under the liner conference block exemption. the repeal of this block exemption will result in lower transport prices, engendering an overall benefit to the eu economy. that said, the commission has also been concerned with preserving the competitiveness of the eu liner shipping industry. that is why we are preparing guidelines explaining how competition law will apply to the liner sector, once regulation (ec) no 4056/86 is repealed. the commission is committed to promulgating the guidelines by the end of 2007. in view of the two-year transitional period, the guidelines will be in place before the repeal of the liner conference block exemption takes effect, thus giving industry ample time to adjust to a new competitive environment in the knowledge that what it seeks to do is lawful. the commission has been discussing closely with both the transport providers, carriers, and the transport users, shippers, on the content of the guidelines. the focus will be on ensuring the competitiveness of the transport sector. i think we all agree that ensuring competitiveness is not the same as shielding the sector from competition. information exchanges are lawful and are common practice in most industries, because they enable business to make better decisions. however, they must not go so far as to prevent undertakings from determining their conduct in the market independently of each other. the process leading to the adoption of the guidelines by the commission includes discussions with both transport users and transport providers, as well as with the member vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. this debate is closely linked to the debate we have just had on structural change in the automobile industry. we agreed that structural change had been with us for a long time and would continue to be so for a long time. i also felt that most people in this room felt that the right answer to structural change was innovation. structural change occurs when a product or process is no longer modern enough. the answer to this cannot be to cut back and leave the field to others, but the answer must be to face this competition through innovation. the commission wants to see the ability and willingness to innovate understood as a guiding political, social and economic principle in the european union. this is not a technical exercise! innovation is indeed something that you first understand in your head and that you have to want. this includes a willingness to accept change. we have put innovation at the heart of our growth and employment strategy for good reason, because a non-protectionist economic order based on freedom cannot survive without innovation. it needs a society that supports and encourages innovation, and it needs a policy framework that encourages innovation. that's what we're doing. we're doing it on two levels. we are doing this at member state level, and it is very important that innovation policies and initiatives are now given a very wide scope in the national reform programmes to implement the lisbon strategy, and the commission will give the highest priority to innovation this year in its review of the lisbon strategy. at european union level, we have already put forward a large number of initiatives recently, all aimed at promoting innovation - from the aid rules, which are now - as was already called for in the debate - specifically geared to innovation, to general financial instruments for the creation of young, innovative companies, to issues of better exploitation of intellectual property and the development of research and development capacities. we are working towards a policy of innovation in one go. i am pleased to report that innovation was the first and foremost topic discussed yesterday at the commission's meeting with the finnish presidency to prepare the programme for the second half of 2006. i am very confident that the finnish presidency is particularly suited to push forward the issue of innovation, because finland is a model example of how a deliberate, targeted and intelligently driven innovation policy can lead to a country's radical modernisation and make it internationally competitive. i always say that we should learn from the good examples of others, so we should do that in this case.

vice-president of the commission. madam president, freedom of association is a general principle of community law and the court of justice has clearly recognised this. there is also an important article, article 12 of the european charter of fundamental rights, which provides for the right to freedom of association at all levels, and particularly in the field of trade unions. freedom of association must therefore always be respected. there is also article 137 of the treaty which states, more specifically, that those same provisions do not apply to the right of association. what is the consequence? there is a freedom of association which is very clearly established in the european charter of fundamental rights, but the treaty does not give the commission the power to intervene, for example against a private company which infringes the right of association. in such cases it is for the national authority, and in particular the judicial authority, to ensure that that right is respected. this is obviously a matter for the courts to decide, simply because there is no concrete rule in the treaty to make a commission power of intervention applicable.

vice-chairman of the commission . mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the suggestions i have received from the debate. i think it can be said that the swift case has a peculiarity, which has led me to say to you today that the 'first pillar' directive of 1995 on data protection is probably the one applicable. this is because the data transfer took place between swift belgium and swift usa, i.e. between two private branches of a private organisation. that is why my interpretation - except of course what the belgian government authorities will tell us - is that the notification to the data protection authority and the national responsibilities of the competent bodies, in this case, would be there. unlike the pnr case, which mr lambrinidis rightly mentions, where there was a transfer between a private airline directly to a us public body, in this case the transfer is between two private parties. and then it happens that on american soil, according to american law, that data transmitted for commercial reasons is used for security purposes. that's the structural difference. the consequence, as mr lambrinidis has pointed out, is that there is a grey area which must be regulated absolutely. there are, in my view, two immediate possibilities: the first, to be implemented with the help of the council and the presidency, is to adopt swiftly the commission's proposal for a framework decision under the third pillar, aimed at protecting the confidentiality of personal data. it is clear that we would have covered at least one area, the one where data is transmitted for security reasons, for investigation, for the fight against terrorism. the first pillar would remain, namely the transition between two private entities for commercial reasons. a third aspect would be missing: the transmission between a member state and a third state, i.e. not data transmitted within the european union to a third state, but from a single member state directly to a third state. this is a third aspect which i think needs to be examined. if we tackle these three points together, which frankly do not concern a dispute with the united states of america but concern all third countries, we can get past that grey area.

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the integration of thirdcountry nationals legally resident in the member states is a permanent challenge for european societies and a key to strengthening their social and political cohesion. the hague programme on freedom, security and justice recognises the importance of integration policy in promoting the stability and cohesion of our societies. the hague programme also mentions the need for better coordination of national policies. in november 2004, the council and the representatives of the governments of the member states adopted conclusions on the establishment of common basic principles for the integration of migrants in the european union. the common basic principles state that integration is a dynamic, two-way process of mutual understanding and adaptation in which all immigrants and residents of the member states participate. member states are therefore encouraged to take account of and include both immigrants and nationals in their integration policies. close interaction between immigrants and nationals of member states is a fundamental means of integration. the common basic principles state in particular that common meeting places for intercultural dialogue, the dissemination of information about immigrants and their cultures and the improvement of living conditions in urban areas improve interaction between immigrants and citizens of the member states. the common basic principles are based on the council conclusions of december 2005, which took into account the commission communication 'a common action plan for integration - a framework for the integration of third-country nationals in the eu'. the communication was issued in september 2005. the importance of integration in the context of the immigration policy of the community and its member states and the need to further develop action in this area have been recognised in a number of initiatives, including the commission's communication on a policy plan on legal immigration. in the above context, it is emphasised that members of the host society must contribute to creating opportunities for migrants to participate in european societies in different ways. this is mutually beneficial for both european citizens and third country nationals. other community actors and institutions, such as the parliament, the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions, can also make a significant contribution to the participation of eu citizens in the integration of third-country nationals in the union.

mr president, i am convinced that the smooth integration of migrants into europe is a challenge equal to this successful enlargement of the union. the more than 40 million immigrants in the union today make up one twenty-sixth of the population of the member states. yet, unlike policies to smooth the integration of candidate countries, the european union has in recent years allocated relatively few staff and money to the great challenge of integrating migrants. the eu council, in his honour, explicitly expressed its commitment to the integration of migrants in tampere in 1999. and he reinforced this position at the thessaloniki summit under the greek presidency in 2003. i would also like to congratulate the commission and mr franco frattini personally on the excellent working document on the integration of immigrants which they adopted a few months ago, with an emphasis on the common basic principles of groningen. but the reality still falls far short of the expectations that have been created. unfortunately, the union has long been paralysed by the widespread view that integration is a local matter and that europe as a whole cannot help it. the integration actions are indeed based on local level. schools, businesses, places of worship, and other agencies of a local community carry out the painstaking work of bringing newcomers and natives together on a daily basis. however, integration is a pan-european issue in terms of its impact, especially when it fails. thus, while local, regional and national authorities must define the precise integration measures in each case, member states as a whole must devise effective integration strategies whose fruits will further the common interests of the union. the european union institutions can and must be much more active and, above all, more effective in monitoring and evaluating these programmes objectively. my report stresses that the integration of immigrants entails both obligations and rights for immigrants and for the citizens of the member states. the report's proposals are based on the need to start consultations on ending the political and social marginalisation of migrants and on encouraging their social and, above all, psychological integration, so that they do not feel condemned to be marginalised. the language of the host country, customs, customs and the functioning of state institutions should be taught to all migrants, while the state should provide them with the opportunity to freely express their cultural identity and equal access to education, jobs, housing, etc. the report stresses, among other things, the importance of adopting positive action measures to integrate immigrants into the educational and employment structures of the member states and into the structures of political parties in the member states. it called on the member states to implement immediately, fairly and without prohibitive restrictions the existing directives on racism and xenophobia, family reunification, equal treatment in employment and longterm resident status. it stresses the importance of providing for the right of citizenship for all longterm immigrants, and in particular for the children of immigrants who have been born and raised among us. it proposes that member states appoint a minister with overall coordinating responsibility for integration and an immigrant advocate. should eu countries take in more immigrants? if so, how many and how? the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. on the contrary, the answer to the question whether we should seek the smooth integration of immigrants already living and working among us is self-evident. they must become full members of our societies. anything less would indicate that we accept and prefer a society of first- and second-class citizens. such a policy would undermine the social and economic fabric of our societies. in other words, it would be unfair and would not benefit anyone. in conclusion, i would like to thank all the political groups, the shadow rapporteurs and the coordinators, and in particular you, patrick, merci beaucoup, because i know how difficult it was for all of us to promote this report. i thank you all for your important amendments to the committee on civil liberties which have made this report stronger and richer. i thank jannine especially for this. i know it hasn't always been easy for all of us to find the perfect combinations, but we've tried and succeeded with many. thank you again.

made a number of proposals in the past few months, some of which have been the subject of your reports and questions. for example, one of the key principles for european action is the principle of solidarity between the member states of the union. this principle implies many things: firstly, it means that the member states undertake to support each other if one of them is subject to particular migratory pressure. the second aspect of the principle of solidarity is precisely what mr gaubert's report deals with and which i very much appreciated. it is a report that arises from a proposal i made in 2005 when i realised the need to make more stable the mutual prior information of each member state that legitimately wanted to take initiatives in the field of immigration, when these initiatives have an impact on other member states. the establishment of a consultation mechanism is another way of applying the principle of solidarity. we must not forget that what happens within the borders of each state has repercussions on other states. this is the mechanism of mutual consultation and information. i welcome all the proposals in mr gaubert's report, including additional proposals such as a permanent political dialogue at ministerial level and also the proposal to have an annual report - which the commission is pleased to present to this parliament every year - on the operation of this mechanism. it was said by those before me: "for this mechanism to work, mutual trust between member states is needed". if there is no mutual trust, we can write the rules, but the rules will just stay on paper". it is therefore necessary to exercise political persuasion with regard to the member states, explaining to them that if they do not communicate, if they do not inform the other states in a real spirit of european sharing, then, as the italian saying goes, 'it may go well for one at a time but it will go badly for another'. so it is in everyone's interest to be totally transparent at all times, and that is the spirit of mr gaubert's report, which i share. what are the broad lines of european immigration policy? firstly, a challenge which must be global and european. secondly - and this is the most innovative aspect - the role of the european union on the international scene as a unique actor, for example and above all in the neighbouring geographical areas, i am referring in particular to africa, the mediterranean area and our neighbours in the east: these are the three major geographical areas where europe must take concrete political action as a single actor in order to have a single voice. within this political challenge, what are the things to do? first, to tackle at european level the root causes of immigration. mr lambert has just said very correctly that: "we must transform migration from desperation into migration by choice of people who freely decide to go to live and work in the european union, but who are not forced to flee because their countries are poor, because there is no drinking water, or because the environment is destroyed. so what do we do? to orient european development aid policies towards strategies that address the lack of local development. for example, targeted interventions in the countries of origin of migration flows to promote investment and the restructuring of the agricultural system or the environmental fabric, which is very often devastated and degraded. we are thinking about projects to be financed together with the world bank to use the remittances of legal immigrants and invest them in their homeland - if they want to, of course. but what's the obstacle? very often immigrants do not have access to bank credit and so in this regard, we want to promote credit services more available to invest, for example, in a small or medium-sized enterprise in a home country. we are developing projects for so-called microcredit to help the recovery of many investment points in the countries of origin. this work will have a global political development, represented by the contribution of europe, which i hope will really speak with one voice, at the september session of the united nations, which is commonly referred to as the high level dialogue on migration and development. this session will take place on the sidelines of the united nations general assembly, it is a session which will focus on the relationship between immigration and the development of the countries of origin, and europe will present - by means of a proposal which i will present to the commission a few days before the summer break - a strategic document, the european commission's contribution to this reflection, which is, i believe, the first issue we must address. the second theme is the fight against human trafficking, as mentioned by mr klamt. you will be aware that human trafficking is now one of the main sources of income for unscrupulous organized crime. we now have very clear information on the traffic flows, the origin of the traffickers and even the price charged to each of the desperate people who are being transported without even a guarantee of arriving alive. on average, traffickers charge these desperate people a huge sum, between $1,500 and $2,500 each, without even a guarantee that they will make it across the mediterranean alive. it is clear that the fight against human trafficking must go hand in hand with the protection of victims of trafficking and therefore with the issue of vulnerable victims, immigrant women, children who are victims of trafficking in illegal immigrants. i believe that in this connection, and this is what we must do, we must also consider a return policy as a european action towards those who cannot remain because they have no right to remain on european territory. i believe that european return operations must be organized by setting standards with the united nations organizations for individual respect, not only for the rights but also for the dignity of these people who must be returned, but they must be returned in full compliance with the standards established by international conventions. in this context we are working on readmission agreements. we have very ambitious challenges at the moment, such as concluding readmission agreements with morocco and then with algeria as soon as possible, once again on a european scale, and no longer on a bilateral basis between states, in order to increase this political dimension of europe. the third theme is legal immigration, which i see as an opportunity, and certainly not as a threat. it is clear that in the area of legal immigration we must respect national rules. it is enough to recall, for example, that even in the constitutional treaty we signed in rome, we made it clear that the number of immigrants who can enter each country is determined at national level, but, having said that, i think that common rules on the admission of legal immigrants are necessary and i fully share the opinion of those who said: "we do not ask for and recruit only highly skilled immigrant workers because we risk impoverishing the countries of origin through the brain drain". our intention is rather to promote circulation because it is clear, as some have said, that many immigrants want to return to their country of origin, to their homeland, and we must help them in this. but then europe needs seasonal workers, agricultural workers, workers in many sectors who are not highly skilled but who are useful and so we can limit ourselves to engineers, doctors or researchers, because that would cause impoverishment in the countries of origin. the fourth theme is integration, and mr lambrinidis knows how much i appreciate his work, and particularly this report, because up to now integration has not been considered for what it really is: this is an integral part of migration policy. i dare say this: "it would be irresponsible to welcome immigrants without integrating them because it would only increase their frustration, their sense of isolation". and it is precisely in this connection that our proposals call for a focus on the key areas of civil rights, housing, education and, of course, regular and not illegal work. we have proposed, and are putting into effect, a permanent european forum for integration, and local governments will have an important say in that forum. how long have we forgotten the mayors, the regional governors, the civil society associations? and when we talk about integration, we cannot think only of the capitals of the member states. the european integration forum will deal with this very issue and i hope that parliament will support the adoption of the european integration fund. it is not a fund that replaces national policies, but one that makes them more efficient. the fifth theme is illegal immigration. i am about to promote an initiative which the commission is expected to adopt on 19 july on certain guidelines for illegal immigration. firstly, i believe that a genuine strategy for education and communication should be promoted in the countries of origin. aspiring immigrants do not know what the rules are when they arrive in europe, they do not know the language, they do not know the job opportunities, they do not know the laws of the european countries which they will have to respect and so why not think, and this is one of the proposals, to vocational training courses, to language courses in the countries of origin that europe can encourage and even co-finance to prepare for legal and necessary immigration. it is clear that if we want to defeat illegal immigration, we must defeat black labour, because black labour is exploitation and it is also a factor of attraction for new illegal immigration. the sixth theme is urgent prevention measures and practical support for member states in greatest difficulty. the mission to the canary islands is decided, thirteen member states have agreed to participate, they will provide naval and air assets for patrolling the atlantic coast in front of the canary islands. a second european mission will then be sent to malta to assist the mediterranean patrol. i believe that these are actions which, for the first time, and i emphasize this again, are coordinated by the frontex agency, that is, by europe. it is not the actions of individual member states that are coming together but there is a european agency that coordinates the work. it is urgently necessary to take measures to patrol and not only that, but also to save lives at sea, because the humanitarian aspect of this immense tragedy is that every week in the mediterranean, in the sea of my country, we see people dying at sea and very often we are not even able to recover their bodies. so these are also absolutely essential actions. finally, the seventh theme, aid to the countries of origin and transit of immigrants. we must give them practical help, we must work with them, and i say this in a spirit which replaces the usual tone of international relations with genuine partnership. i am about to attend the rabat conference which will take place on monday and tuesday next week, in morocco. at this conference, for the first time, african countries and europe will meet to work out a joint action plan. i believe that we will then need to create a tool for the constant monitoring of the initiatives we will take in the next few days and that a second meeting will then be necessary, this time with the aegis of the african union. i believe that the future is the african union and the european union through a strategic programme. i think this could really make a difference.

member of the commission. mr president, i certainly share the desire of the chairman of the committee on international trade that this very regrettable development in the negotiations should be a temporary halt, rather than an indefinite suspension. i welcome the fact that he and other members of this house are meeting other parliamentarians from wto member countries to review this matter. the more we can gain a broad understanding of what is at stake and what the problems are, and the more we can spread that knowledge amongst the players in the various wto countries – rather than keeping this knowledge to a very tightly-knit circle of negotiators – then the better off we will be. i will certainly pursue that objective when i visit washington dc later this month to meet with leading figures on the hill. the last time i discussed the doha development agenda with some of the members of this house was in geneva in late june. first of all i would like to say how much i appreciated your presence there, your networking activities and the way in which you played an interesting and useful role among the negotiating parties. we will need your backing in the future in our efforts to convince our wto partners to resume these negotiations, and i very strongly commend the approach taken by the members of this house. at the end of the week i will travel to rio de janeiro at the invitation of the government of brazil and the g20 group of developing countries. this will be the first chance to review at ministerial level what happened in geneva in july, to discuss our respective positions and to assess the possibility of how and when we can move forward. in the weeks following the suspension, all sides have expressed a commitment to seeing the round succeed. nobody is saying, on the face of it at any rate, that they are no longer committed to it, and doha certainly needs that level of commitment. in all our actions and statements we need to top up confidence in the round and the process and to reassert the values of multilateralism and the economic benefits of a wide and ambitious deal. however, the rhetoric has to be matched with political leadership. what we are faced with is a lack of what one might call ‘realistic ambition’. all sides are exporting their domestic constraints into these negotiations. perhaps that is inevitable, but it is not or should not be allowed to become an excuse for failure. yet even in the most difficult and seemingly intractable areas of negotiation, the positions on agriculture are not that divergent. they are not so far apart that they are irreconcilable. they dictate that the eu lift its average tariff cut close to that requested by the g-20 developing countries. the eu signalled in geneva that it was willing to negotiate on that as part of a balanced package – if others too are prepared to move forwards and show the same sort of flexibility we ourselves are demonstrating. if we are to move in the direction i have indicated we could, then in the right circumstances, this would represent a substantial shift from our original offer of a 39% average farm tariff cut, which is already much higher than the cuts accepted in the uruguay round. these would be the steepest farm tariff cuts ever accepted as part of a multilateral trade negotiation. nobody could describe this as ‘doha-light’. to these can be added the subsidy cuts flowing from eu reform, which would see eu producers withdraw dramatically from key global export markets such as milk and poultry, and the contraction of the eu grain market as demand for animal feed falls. if one puts all that together it amounts to a major new market access package for competitive agricultural exporters such as the united states, australia and other members of the cairns group. it would potentially downsize european agriculture by up to usd 20 billion per year. to dismiss this as insignificant, as some have done, is either a crude negotiating posture or a failure to do the necessary maths. in return for those cuts, the eu is looking to the united states to match it in cutting trade-distorting farm subsidies, which the developing world now rightly regards as the condition and catalyst for any final doha agreement. the united states has offered significant cuts in the so-called ‘amber box’ trade-distorting subsidies, from usd 19.1 billion down to usd 7.6 billion. this sounds good, and is to be welcomed. however, the united states has also proposed an increase in what it is allowed to spend in other categories of trade-distorting subsidy, while rejecting the idea of directly reforming those subsidy programmes so as to ensure that they no longer distort trade. if one adds together the three types of proposed trade-distorting support that the united states wants to keep, one actually arrives at a potential new ceiling of usd 22.7 billion, which is more than the united states currently spends. in other words, by the end of the doha implementation period, us trade-distorting payments to farmers could actually go up as a result of what the us tabled in its offer last october. it is understandable that the us’s trading partners have found that unacceptable, especially given the sweeping cuts that the us is demanding from others, in terms both of subsidies and tariffs. quite rightly, developing countries are insisting on an effective reduction in us subsidies, and the eu supports that. unless there is a shift in the us position, advanced developing countries such as brazil and india will not be prepared to offer greater access to their markets for industrial goods and services, and that is the crux of the eventual deal we are seeking. that deal will be hard to reach. i do not underestimate the difficulties that will arise in the negotiations we are yet to have with the advanced developing countries on industrial tariffs. however, it is the stand-off on agriculture, which represents only a fraction of trade for developing and developed countries alike, that is preventing the doha negotiations from addressing trade in manufacturing and services, which is where the vast bulk of the potential economic gains from this round lie. we will only achieve closure on doha if all the parties involved make the effort to sell an outcome on its merits across all areas of the negotiations. these include not only agriculture and farm tariffs, but also manufacturing, services and rules. all sides should realise that a realistically ambitious and achievable outcome, far from being a ‘doha-light’, would actually yield deep-seated structural changes in farm policies and create new trade flows in goods and services on a scale unmatched in any previous trade rounds. in other words, there is an awful lot already on the table, as mr lamy has repeatedly pointed out. what is being lost in a continued stalemate – let us be clear about this – is being lost first and foremost by developing countries. it is they who are losing new trade opportunities. even more importantly, they risk losing out as a result of a weakening of the multilateral trading system. we on the eu side will try to do as much as we possibly can, in any scenario, for the weaker and more vulnerable developing countries, without seeking to divide the wto membership. in particular, we will keep our promises on aid for trade, and we will maintain our efforts. some will ask how it is that suspension of the dda will affect our broader trade policy stance. the answer is that our commitment to doha will remain paramount. nothing can replace the wto. firstly, it is based on equality and the rule of law, rather than on raw power. secondly, some benefits can only be achieved in a multilateral context, such as new disciplines on farm or fishery subsidies, a new agreement on trade facilitation, new disciplines for anti-dumping tools and better and clearer rules on regional trade agreements. these are examples of areas where any number of bilateral agreements could not even begin to achieve the sort of improvement and strengthening of trade rules and the trade system that we are seeking. thirdly, these are the only form of negotiations in which smaller developing countries can punch their collective political weight. finally, the dispute settlement system itself is one of the cornerstones of the wto system and a feature unique in international law. there is no doubt that any erosion of confidence in the multilateral trading system as a whole would in the long term also critically affect that dispute settlement system. bilateral and regional deals are therefore not an alternative to multilateral negotiations, but rather an add-on and a complement that helps to address in greater depth a reduction in tariff and non-tariff barriers, as well as establishing disciplines in areas in which wto members have decided – at least for the time being – not to negotiate collectively within the multilateral system, be it in relation to competition rules, government procurement or the labour dimension. we are looking at several negotiations in this context. some are already in progress, while others will be launched when the conditions are ripe. mercosur, the gcc and central america are in the first group and we are also looking at ukraine, india, korea and the asean countries as potential partners for new initiatives. let me conclude by saying that i and the commission remain firmly committed to a successful outcome of the multilateral round and that i want to work closely with you in this house to achieve that goal. that remains my priority. the commission will also shortly present soon two communications – one in october on external aspects of our competitiveness in europe, and one on trade relations with china. these will tackle other key issues of our future trade policy. i am keen to discuss both of these with you in the coming weeks, and look forward to doing so. as a team i believe we should continue to work together in the future as well as we have done in the past – for europe’s sake, but also for the benefit of the global economy and in particular for the most needy developing countries. representative of parliament or of the committee on international trade as a whole, and i hope it is not. the commission consults parliament on all main trade policy orientations on the basis of the westerterp procedure which, as we know, provides for the possibility of a debate in parliament before the opening of negotiations on any trade agreement, as well as for information from the council before the conclusion of any such agreement. we do so also on the basis of the stuttgart declaration, which states that parliament should be consulted on the conclusion of all agreements – even ones covered by the then article 113 – that have an important bearing on the community. our commitment to this relationship is shown by the fact that we send the committee on international trade copies of all the policy documents that are under discussion in the council’s article 133 committee. there is no legal obligation on us to do this. we do it because it is right and because it helps underpin our relations. no doubt we could do even better in the future, but to characterise what we do at the moment as ‘poor’ or ‘insufficient’ seems inaccurate. a number of the points raised relate to legitimate concerns over the impact of these negotiations – both their direction and suspension – on developing countries. i should make it clear that developing countries do not conform to a ‘standard size’ state of development or set of interests when it comes to the negotiations. there are different developing countries with very different interests and very different needs. our job is primarily to ensure two things: firstly, that all developing countries benefit and gain from these negotiations and, secondly, that the weaker, more vulnerable and less-developed among them receive the greatest direct assistance, not least in terms of capacity-building, aid for trade and the putting in place of a full duty-free and quota-free system that enables them to access rich world markets. in other words, we operate a system of proportionality: proportionality vis-à-vis what we expect developing countries to contribute and the effort we expect of them in bringing these negotiations to a conclusion, and proportionality also in terms of what we give and how we support and underpin their development. the countries that are in greatest need and have least to offer are quite rightly those which are, and will remain, our priority in these negotiations. it is important to stress this because, unlike some of those who have spoken, i passionately believe that a good doha deal can contribute to development and to fairer trade, through the way in which we operate special and differential treatment between developing countries, the way we allow carve-outs for commitments to developing countries to protect and enable the development of infant industry, the way we provide for longer implementation periods for developing countries so that they can prepare for change and, in particular, the way that we grant special access to the least-developed countries and attention to their capacity needs. we shall continue to adhere to that standard, as you would expect us to do, throughout the negotiations. what is important is to have not just access for developing countries to the markets of the developed world, but also much greater access for developing countries to the markets of other developing countries. what is important is south-south trade, especially given the extent of duty-free and quota-free access that we in europe already give to developing countries and particularly the acp countries, as a result of which 75% of agricultural exports from africa come to europe, as do 45% of those from latin america. in fact, we are the most open and fair-minded trading bloc in the world. let us remember that fact, whilst also reminding ourselves of what we can do better in the future. the greatest and earliest gains for developing countries will come from increased trade opportunities with other developing countries. it is therefore south-south trade that we must not lose sight of when delicately and sensitively addressing the issues of tariff reductions and the much-needed multilateralisation of ‘everything but arms’. others who have spoken have suggested that far from giving too little for and to developing countries, the european negotiating position has consisted of giving far too much, too early and showing far too much flexibility. well, we in europe conceived the doha round. we were primarily instrumental in launching it and we have nurtured it throughout. after cancún we were instrumental in putting it back on track, through the framework agreement, in 2004, and i do not apologise for putting an end date, in hong kong, on the elimination of our export subsidies. this was a commitment we had already made, assuming, of course, that we reach the end of these negotiations and that other countries act similarly in eliminating the components of their export subsidisation. i make no apology, and am not actually primarily responsible for the future of the common agricultural policy, although i would point out that i do not as yet see a consensus emerging in favour of its abolition. in the event of a doubtful outcome to the doha negotiations, we will have to look very carefully at what happens to the future of export subsidies, because that is linked to another point that has been raised in this debate – i.e. whether or not we will be more or less vulnerable to litigation at the wto in cases brought against us on agriculture should a deal not be reached in the multilateral negotiations. if these negotiations do not succeed, i agree that it is likely that there will be an upsurge in cases brought to the purposes and needs, as well as for the needs of others within the international trading system. to the extent that we have now implemented that reform, and will continue to do so, we are protected vice-president of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i should first of all like to point out that the commission has no direct competence in the area of bankruptcy legislation. nevertheless, this area is particularly important for small and mediumsized enterprises and the commission is therefore trying to play a mediating role here. we have made sure that best practice is made public and have encouraged member states to introduce best practice. the commission sees its work as focusing on preventing insolvencies and promoting restructuring, not on winding up companies. we are working on more business-friendly rules for non-fraudulent insolvencies and finally we are dealing with the question of support for a new start, that is to say, the question of second chance. the european charter for small enterprises points out that some insolvencies can occur even if the initiative is responsible and if entrepreneurial risks are taken. accordingly, a review of national insolvency laws in the light of best practice is required. various steps have been taken in this regard. in spring 2001 a seminar on business failure was held in noordwijk. the main issues were the improvement of bankruptcy laws and the prevention of insolvencies. the study bankruptcy and a fresh start, which collects data on the legal and social consequences of business insolvencies, was published in mid-2002. this study forms the basis of the commission's best project 'restructuring, bankruptcy and a new start' of 2003, which focused on two key issues: how far does national insolvency law prevent a company from continuing to exist and from starting over? how does the stain of failure affect the chances of success in the relaunch of failed businesses and the entrepreneurial spirit in general? the results of this project were presented in a report which was intended to support the trend in european policy towards changing the legal framework of bankruptcy laws. the main recommendations and benchmarks ranged from emphasising the usefulness of external advice in preventing insolvency, to the importance of current and reliable insolvency laws in facilitating conciliation and restructuring, to the importance of a clear distinction between fraudulent and non-fraudulent bankruptcy and the corresponding allocation of different legal consequences. the report has indeed contributed to a strengthening of the pan-european effort to reform insolvency law. in response to some comments on the green paper 'entrepreneurship in europe', the commission extended the entrepreneurship action plan in 2004 to include a focused action on business insolvency with three specific objectives. first, the commitment of the member states to implement the recommendations of the final report of the expert group on restructuring, bankruptcy and new start. secondly, better understanding of business failure, thirdly, promotion of preventive measures for companies in the danger zone. in relation to objectives 2 and 3, the commission is currently developing an information kit and self-assessment tests for entrepreneurs to identify early business risk factors when the prospects for remediation are still good, as part of the multiannual project 'stigma of failure and early warning tools'. on 28 march 2006, the commission organised a conference in brussels on 'insolvency and a new start'. this conference focused on methods of preventing insolvency, combating the stigma of a failed enterprise and promoting a new start after non-fraudulent business insolvencies. there are positive signs of implementation of these priorities at national level. the national reform programmes submitted by around one third of the member states under the lisbon strategy - which also includes greece - included plans for the reform of national insolvency law for 2005.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, today is an important day for me personally, but also for my colleagues and the committee on culture and education, because after almost a year of work, i have the pleasure of presenting to the house my report on the protection of europe's natural, architectural and, in general, cultural heritage in rural and island areas. for centuries, with simple materials and means, the inhabitants of the countryside and islands of europe, obeying the basic rules of human scale and the gentleness of the natural environment, have managed to create a built heritage of great aesthetic value. this humble heritage, whose protection and promotion is not only a cultural duty but also a development imperative, has been seriously damaged in many european countries by the responsibility of governments, as a result of social and technological developments, excessive economic exploitation and over-construction, which have led to the deterioration of the landscape and the destruction - especially on the small scale of islands - of the marvellous balance between the natural and built environment and, on the other hand, to the destruction of highly productive agricultural land. my report aims to make concrete proposals for the protection, enhancement and long-term management of this rich heritage of europe's countryside and islands for the benefit of the quality of life of all european citizens. the proposals in the report are addressed to the european union, the member states, local and regional authorities and european citizens who are called upon to take concrete measures to preserve and promote it. because of the limited time, i'll just focus on a few of them: firstly, it is necessary for the union to have a comprehensive strategy for cultural heritage. this will be achieved if the european commission, when drawing up its legislative proposals, considers thoroughly the impact of the proposed legislation on culture, cultural heritage and in particular the folk architectural heritage created by the hand of the folk craftsman over the centuries. in this way, actions in favour of heritage will be integrated into all union policies. as community programmes in the field of culture do not provide sufficient funding, additional resources for heritage conservation should be sought in other community instruments: the common agricultural policy, the structural funds, and the community initiatives leader, urban and interreg, which are to be integrated in the next financial period into the new financial instruments of cohesion policy and the cap. in addition, using community funds, member states should encourage alternative sustainable tourism, which can be a factor in protecting and promoting the architectural heritage of housing estates that have retained most of their character. the culture programme, with its limited budget, has also largely supported projects promoting cultural heritage, but excluding funding for restoration. however, there are other actions which could be funded under the new culture 2007 programme. in particular, a network of architecturally significant settlements from different member states with a population of up to 1000 inhabitants could be created under the multiannual cooperation projects of the programme. these settlements will carry out cultural activities in accordance with the traditions of each region in order to strengthen cooperation between the architecturally and culturally remarkable settlements of europe and to give them the opportunity to highlight their local peculiarities, customs, customs and traditions. the european commission is also called upon to create a new european institution for small, valuable traditional settlements, similar to the 'cultural capitals', where one or two interesting settlements will be selected each year for restoration and rehabilitation interventions and cultural events throughout the year. in order to highlight the architecturally significant housing estates in europe, we also propose the creation, within the framework of the 'european union prize for cultural heritage', of a new category of prize to be awarded to the best overall restoration of a traditional housing estate. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, europe's built environment, which is made up of sub-assemblies of different architectural styles and periods, is being seriously altered by the over-construction of buildings, and by the existence of incompatible structures which do not correspond to the particular architectural characteristics of the historical area in which they are located. the member states must therefore provide incentives for the partial or total withdrawal of such buildings, while at the same time it is necessary not to support with community funds projects which have been shown to result in the destruction and alteration of important elements of the cultural heritage. finally, the report also proposes that the european union establish a 'european year of cultural heritage' to raise awareness among european citizens of the importance of cultural heritage, regardless of its european, national or local dimension. in conclusion, i would like to thank in particular the secretariat of the committee on culture, the experts who have worked with me and, of course, my colleagues in the committee on culture.
mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to congratulate my compatriot, mr seefunakis, on his very good work. the cultural heritage, commissioner, is an important element of the identity and historical development of the peoples of europe. the protection and preservation of these sites is therefore of particular importance for the education of the younger generation and for respecting european identity, which, apart from its european dimension, is a fundamental value for european citizens. we all find that the spotlight is on the big cities where the most famous monuments are located. however, it is a fact that the european countryside, which represents 90% of the european territory, is suffering from neglect and economic decline. special care should therefore be taken to protect and promote the natural and architectural cultural heritage of island and other rural areas of europe, as these areas retain their characteristics largely unchanged. all actors active in the cultural field must ensure that europe's cultural heritage is preserved and exploited, while respecting the traditional rural environment and ensuring a balance between the population and the environment, and raising awareness of its importance among citizens. the restoration and preservation of forgotten monuments in the regions of the member states could also contribute to the development of rural tourism and, by extension, to the population of the countryside. finally, the recognition and preservation of the common cultural heritage is therefore an important legacy for future generations.
