in writing. the kke votes against the report because, despite the improvements it proposes in the european commission's proposal for a directive, it accepts in essence its basic philosophy as a whole, which is none other than the unlimited and practically uncontrollable possibility of the prosecuting authorities and repressive mechanisms not only of the eu member states but also of third countries (say the usa), even private individuals (!) to collect, process and exchange among themselves all the personal data of every eu citizen, including data concerning his political and trade union activity, his ideological, philosophical and religious beliefs! the eu's giant "cover" mechanism is now targeting every eu citizen, allowing the collection and transfer of personal data of any person without even being suspected of any act, simply for reasons of public order and security!! the right to privacy and the protection of personal data is effectively abolished, since the proposed directive on the so-called protection of personal data establishes exceptions to this protection as the rule, simply and unchecked by the invention of public security reasons, while data protection is the exception, which is almost impossible to enforce.
in writing. the report is moving towards the harmonisation of the rules of criminal procedure and the 'communitisation' of criminal law at eu level, in the context of the implementation of the hague programme for the creation of a single 'safe area of freedom and justice'. the committee also calls for the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the european parliament and the council are able to take account of the views of the european parliament and the council on the future of the union. in this way, eu law adds another tool to the effort to impose on national criminal laws the eu's supranational regulations which define the behaviour which it considers to be punishable. it is another step towards tightening the noose around individual freedoms, it targets the action of the mass popular movement and creates the conditions for the militant activities of the movement to be characterized as punishable. the kke opposes the report and calls on workers to step up their action, through the labour and wider popular movement, to defend democratic rights and popular freedoms.
in writing. public services, with their separation into economic and non-economic services, are targeted by big capital in order to commercialise the satisfaction of basic needs and increase the profitability of the public sector. the eu is strengthening its prohibition of state aid under the pretext of protecting competition, and is promoting the full liberalisation and privatisation of services in order to allow the penetration of large capital. in the context of the single market and the stability pact, member states sell off the wealth of the people by strengthening the plutocracy. the eu says capital-efficient services must be sold off. the effects of this policy will be particularly painful for the workers. thousands of jobs lost, working conditions worsened, living standards fell. the consequences for all users of these services, and particularly for the lower classes, will be particularly negative. the consequences are already apparent in services which have been 'victims' of capitalist restructuring and privatisation policies. the committee voted against the resolution which accepted the separation of the economic and non-economic services of the ecsc and encouraged the sale and commercialisation of these services. it sympathizes with workers who are fighting for better and cheaper public services for the benefit of the people's living standards and not for monopoly profits.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i fully agree with the conclusions of the minister, who represents the presidency. i think that no one in this house has any doubts about the catastrophic scale of the darfur tragedy, nor can there be any doubt that it is, in essence, a genuine genocide. but today's debate touches on a much more general political issue, one of the greatest importance for this parliament and for the institutions of the european union in general, namely the role of the european union as the promoter and defender of fundamental rights outside its own borders. we often ask ourselves whether the european union can and should - i believe it can and should - be the bearer in the world of the fundamental rights of respect for human dignity first and foremost, a human dignity which is completely erased by the tragedy of darfur, but to do this the great political debate we have to face is how europe can take these values beyond its borders and defend them if we have interlocutors like the sudanese government, which tolerates and encourages fundamentalism and the harshest and most horrible measures taken by the militias. well, many of you have said, quite bluntly, "let us go with soldiers and weapons, let us apply article 7, let us bring a military force that will forcefully put an end to this catastrophic situation". i am well aware that this is one of the possibilities provided for in the international treaties, but i wonder: 'we europeans have often spoken of ensuring, precisely in promoting human rights in the world, the so-called ownership principle, in other words we cannot impose, by deciding here in strasbourg or brussels, what is the right way to go for another country or for another continent.' we must work with local institutions, and in my view the first recipe is to work with the african union, strengthening its role, ensuring that it is given concrete help, that we do not see a europe in the distance and then suddenly there to promote with soldiers and weapons a role that, if anything, the african union must strengthen and empower. this is the first step, as the presidency has just said, and the second step will be logistical aid on the ground. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission is not prepared to take action in this area. how can we ensure that humanitarian aid actually reaches the people who need it, the suffering population, the ngos on the ground who risk their lives? so logistical support on the ground is another area where we as the european union can make a difference. the third step, and some have remembered it too little, is how to work with the arab league. in many parts of the world, we are confronted with the sensibilities of islamic or arab countries, which in some cases are our strong allies, for example in the fight against terrorism, and in other cases show such a heightened sensibility that they advise us to reach agreements before we intervene. what's the difference between darfur and lebanon? the difference is that lebanon had the agreement and the soldiers went as peace-keeping because the lebanese government and the israeli government together agreed. the sudanese government continues to refuse. do you think it is possible to intervene unilaterally without a decisive role for the arab league? do you not think that in that large population which unfortunately supports the most fundamentalist ideas in the world, such an action, without a strong role for the arab league, would send an extremely negative signal of strengthening the extremists and fundamentalists, who would have an additional propaganda argument? the third recipe is the arab league. we are working to encourage the arab league to disengage from the sudanese government, to withdraw its consent and support; and that's partly what's happening, as you know, and we need to work more in that direction. there is another theme that someone has brought up: "but if the government in khartoum does not listen to the calls of the international community, what happened?" i have always been of the opinion that military action, even if humanitarian intervention is justified by article 7 of the treaty, is still an extreme ratio. there are other intermediate steps, and in this connection i have heard someone evoke the "no-fly zone": it is a measure that could be explored, adopted and proposed. you know that if we were to propose to the security council an article 7 action, china, whether we like it or not, would probably veto it and so nothing would happen. so i ask myself: "isn't it better to work on an initiative, perhaps not decisive but useful, like blocking the overflight of planes, which bring death, which bomb, which strike? " this is another real possibility. i shall conclude with two points. the first: president barroso and his colleague louis michel will go to khartoum. they will send a strong message to the highest authorities of the sudanese government that the european union intends to take strong diplomatic action, but also on the ground, to help the suffering people. the message will reflect on the isolation sudan would face if it continued to refuse to listen to the international community, which would be devastating to sudan itself: there is no point in khartoum being isolated from the rest of the international community, and that would, ladies and gentlemen, remove the alibi for president bashir to maintain such a negative attitude. another very important point on which the commission will be speaking will be the role of women and children. we talk about it a lot here in europe, we deal with victims of trafficking, forced prostitution; we have identified a european road map for children's rights. it is clear that we cannot turn a blind eye to the rights of women and children outside europe in a dramatic case such as that of darfur. so i personally hope that this parliament will make a firm stand in its action on darfur precisely for the special protection of women and children who are, as always, the most vulnerable victims.

berlin on 18 september 2006, he indicated that the central strand of the october trade policy review would argue that the eu should seek to build on and complement its commitment to the multilateral trading system with a new generation of bilateral free trade agreements with key growing markets. while europe continues to be highly competitive in global export markets, european companies are losing ground in the highest technology products and the fastest growing markets. in rapidly growing regions such as asia, the european union is underperforming. there is now a case for new bilateral free trade agreements designed to deliver more open markets. ftas can build on wto multilateral liberalisation by addressing areas, such as trade and services, public procurement and competition policy, that are not yet fully addressed by wto rules. in this respect, the deepening of eu-india bilateral trade relations supports the larger multilateral trading regime. finally, as many of you have said during the discussion, strengthening eu-india relations represents a great hope: that of reducing the wealth gap existing in that country, of improving the conditions for workers and ensuring better standards of protection for all workers, in particular for women and children, and of improving the quality of life of the indian people in general which, as has rightly been pointed projects for the acquisition of informatics equipment in schools or public organisations in the regions, including remote, island or mountainous areas. as you also know, greece has started the implementation of a major project aimed at extending broadband access to those greek regions outside athens and thessaloniki which do not yet have that connection and, under normal commercial circumstances, would not get it. the greek government has also launched the diodos project, which established a high-capacity greek internet educational network through which a number of internet providers are offering advanced internet services to research, academic and education communities at prices that are expected to be 50% below current retail prices. you will also be aware that the commission is working very hard on bridging the digital divide. that is why the commission recently published a communication on bridging the broadband gap, which gives a strong commitment to achieve broadband for all europeans through policy, budget aid and regulatory instruments. included in that are the structural funds, but also – and this is new – the rural funds, in full respect of state aid rules. the communication proposes action that aims at strengthening current policies, national broadband strategies and reinforcing the exchange of best practices through a website. we believe it is very important for the regions to understand what other regions have done and to see what they might be able to copy or adapt to their specific needs. in that sense we hope that the many problems that persist in some regions, and especially in greece, can gradually be overcome.

member of the commission. my answer to the honourable member is that, according to information from the registry, the number of applications submitted during the sunrise period was 346 218, of which 181 306 were filed during the first phase and 164 912 during the second. the current rate of rejection for applications from ireland is 46%, compared to an overall eu rejection rate of 34%. the complete table with a breakdown of all applications per prior right and country of applicant can be found on the registry’s website. the kind of documentary evidence to be provided by an applicant depends on the national law of the member state in which the prior right is established. there are huge differences between the legal systems of the member states, which are reflected in the more or less complicated means needed to prove the existence of a prior right. this results in a higher or lower rate of rejection of applications in certain countries, such as ireland. as to the question of whether the registry provided irish registrars with the necessary means to comply fully with the application process, the commission is not aware of any specific discrimination in this respect. from october 2005 – that is, two months before the launch of the sunrise period – the registry published on its website and in all the official languages a detailed description of all technical and administrative measures concerning the registration procedures. this information, by the way, is still available online to any interested party. during that same period, the registry also set up a call centre, where applicants could obtain quick responses to their questions in 20 official languages. as to the alternative dispute resolution procedure, its purpose is promptly to resolve disputes between domain name holders on matters such as cyber-squatting or intellectual property rights, as well as in relation to individual decisions by the registry. should an irish applicant consider that he or she falls within either of these two categories, the commission is of the opinion that the alternative dispute resolution procedure is indeed a fair method for remedying the problem. in conclusion, the commission considers that the information made available by the public registry is sufficient for applicants and for registrars to proceed with the registration of domain names during the registration period and afterwards.
member of the commission. according to the legal framework established for the dot.eu registry, the commission is not responsible for deciding on the interpretation of national law in connection with the validation of prior rights. that mission has been assigned to the validation agent selected by the registry, pricewaterhouse coopers. that is one point. the second point is that the decision was also taken, in collaboration with the european parliament, to be respectful of national law in that sense; and because there are huge differences between national laws, i would not like to say that one law is better than the other. national law is linked to national habits, to the cultural diversity of our countries, so it is up to the national governments to change this law or to leave it as it is.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your support. i am pleased to open this joint discussion on the thematic strategy for the protection and conservation of the marine environment and on the proposed directive on marine strategy. i would like to thank both rapporteurs, mrs lienemann for the proposed directive on the marine strategy and mr kuskissi for the thematic strategy, and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection for their efforts. i would also like to thank the committee on fisheries and in particular mr gklavakis for his very constructive approach to this important subject. seas and oceans cover 71% of the earth's surface and account for 90% of the biosphere. europe's sea waters cover 3 million square kilometres, the same area as the continent. 50% of europe's territory is covered by the sea. marine ecosystems play a key role in climate and weather. however, the state of the marine environment in the european union is deteriorating rapidly. in some areas, we can go so far that there's no going back. the marine ecology of the baltic sea is strongly influenced by nutrient supply. fish stocks are in poor condition all over europe. the north-east atlantic is one of the most maritime-intensive areas in the world, with all the associated risks and impacts. the mediterranean is highly threatened by uncontrolled coastal development. however, existing measures and efforts, whether at international, national or eu level, are far from sufficient to change the situation. most measures developed at eu level are not designed to protect the marine environment as such and therefore have limited impact. measures adopted at international level have proved to be very difficult to implement and enforce because they are not binding. a healthy marine environment is essential to life as such and to the quality of our lives. it is also a prerequisite for the full exploitation of the economic potential of the oceans and seas, and a dynamic marine economy can only thrive if there is a healthy marine environment. the maritime strategy will therefore make a significant contribution to the growth and employment requirements of the lisbon strategy. for these reasons, it is clear that the protection of the marine environment can no longer and must not be a by-product of other policies. an integrated strategy is needed at eu level to take account of all pressures and impacts on the marine environment. and that is what the marine thematic strategy is trying to achieve. it consists of a draft directive on a marine strategy and a communication explaining the current situation, taking into account the eu's environmental footprint in the marine environment in a broader sense and explaining why the eu needs to act. the maritime strategy needs to be seen in the wider context of the development of the new eu maritime policy. the commission's green paper, adopted in june this year, aims to achieve a europe with a dynamic maritime economy that is compatible with the marine environment. the marine strategy is a pillar of future maritime policy in the environmental field. it will focus on activities needed to protect marine ecosystems, on which sustainable wealth, productivity and employment, and more broadly, human wealth derived from the oceans and seas, depend. the proposed marine strategy directive aims to achieve 'good environmental status' of the eu marine environment by 2021, in other words to restore the ecological health of our seas over the next 15 years. this timeline will coincide with the first review of river basin management plans under the eu water framework directive, allowing synergies in the further implementation of both directives. the joint implementation of the eu water framework directive and the marine strategy directive will thus link the protection of the marine and inland water environment. based on geographical and environmental criteria, the directive establishes european marine regions and identifies sub-regions, if any, as the management units for implementation. no action will be taken at eu level with regard to the procedure. in the first phase, member states will be tasked with developing marine strategies at the level of regional seas and proposing concrete solutions to meet the specific needs of these seas. marine strategies should primarily include an assessment of the state of the marine environment, its threats and impacts, environmental objectives and indicators, and monitoring programmes. in the second phase, member states will be responsible for developing and implementing measures to achieve good environmental status. cooperation between member states and with third countries with which member states share marine waters will be essential. to achieve this, member states will have to work within the framework of regional sea conventions. regional conventions are invaluable partners in the implementation of the strategy. this is demonstrated by the long-standing experience of these conventions both in terms of scientific and technical capabilities and qualifications, but also in terms of the demonstrated ability to work effectively at regional level. in conclusion, i would like to stress the importance and the sensitivity of marine ecosystems. a high level of protection of the marine environment is a prerequisite for exploiting the full economic potential of the oceans and seas. the marine environment is indeed a fundamental resource of our maritime economy. the marine environment is in danger. the eu must therefore act effectively. i hope that the strategy we have proposed will contribute to that.
the committee on fisheries adopted an opinion on the proposal. the main objective of the proposed directive, mr president, is to achieve a good state of the marine environment. this strategy is more urgent today than ever, because the marine ecosystem has been seriously degraded. but for this strategy to be effective, we need to be aware of two or three things. first of all, back home, we say if you don't crack eggs, you don't make an omelet. the money allocated to this action is very small. the commission has already proposed a new approach to the problem of the use of the euro in the european union. i think that is not enough. saving our seas is such a serious matter that it's worth spending more money. secondly, we need to coordinate our actions. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishermen are not caught by the fishermen themselves. we must reach out to them, convince them that they must first of all protect the environment. but not only; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the third point i would like to make is the one that was raised by commissioners borg and dimas. what is this ? that we should agree on some common indicators to measure the state of the environment at the moment, so that - and this is very important - when we talk about good state of the marine environment, we mean the same thing. so we have to agree on common metrics. in conclusion, i would like to say and emphasize that the directive on the marine strategy must give fisheries the importance it deserves and put it at the centre of the effort.

member of the commission. madam president, in accordance with the principles of institutional and procedural autonomy which underpin the ec treaty, it is for each member state to determine which courts are responsible for competition matters. most member states, as you are aware, have specific procedural rules for competition-related issues and these include, for example, referring these cases directly to higher courts, limiting the number or type of competent courts or using specialist courts. national courts also have at their disposal a number of mechanisms in case of doubt about the application of article 81 and article 82 to a proceeding. in particular, further to article 15 of regulation 1/2003, national courts can ask the commission for its opinion on any question on the interpretation of the ec competition rules raised by the facts of a case. so far the national courts have done so in some twenty cases. if a binding interpretation of the rules is sought, the national court can refer to the court of justice under the preliminary ruling procedure and a number of member states also provide for the possibility for the courts to refer awkward questions to the national competition authorities. the commission, of course, welcomes all initiatives taken by member states to increase the expertise of the national judiciary in ec competition law. the commission itself has already cofinanced the training of approximately 1900 judges on the application of ec competition laws.

related to the unequal representation of women, we have chosen their elimination as another key objective for our programme. amongst the commission’s strategic actions for the next five years, the establishment of a european network of women in economic and political decision-making can be highlighted, as well as awareness-raising campaigns, data collection, analysis and exchange of good vice-president of the commission. mr president, i have to admit that this discussion has left me a bit puzzled. in the white paper on a new communication policy, we have tried, first of all, to analyse the problem with previous communication policies and see exactly what we have to do to ensure that we democratically safeguard citizens’ rights to information and ensure they have a say in decision-making in europe. we established five areas of action. we need to define common principles, such as freedom of expression, diversity, inclusion, participation. we need to empower citizens. we need to involve them in different ways, from civic education, giving them a basic knowledge of what goes on, to engaging with civil society. we cannot ignore the new media and new technologies. if we think that it is enough to publish an article in the financial times to communicate with citizens, i am sorry, this is 2006. the debate is also shaped elsewhere. the real divide, as someone said at one of our stakeholder conferences, is between the decision-makers and those who use the internet. if you look at the campaign in france, most of the websites on the constitution were ‘no’ websites. where were those who wanted to argue for a ‘yes’ vote? they did not use the internet enough. we have to understand and embrace what is going on in the new technologies. the fourth chapter is understanding public opinion. we have to be more professional in monitoring and linking up to public opinion. as many of you have said, we have to do the job together. all the institutions have to take responsibility. in this debate, some have accused us of issuing propaganda as soon as we do anything and others seem to think that it is enough to increase the number of europe direct information points in europe. that will not do. we have to have a serious communication policy as a tool for democracy, a tool for citizens. they have a right to better understanding. they have a right to participate in a public sphere where we have a truly european political culture and truly pan-european media, reflecting the debate that is going on and helping us to understand and follow it. we also need to establish meeting places for citizens where they can participate. you say we already have democracy in europe. well, we have a participatory deficit. the majority of citizens still say they know very little or do not know enough about the european union and its institutions, they are not able to follow what is being done in the european parliament or the commission. can we simply say that we do not care and continue with business as usual? we have to change the way we communicate with citizens and it is their right to engage with us. we will continue to work on all the things that you have mentioned. we have steadily increased the europe direct centres. we now have 400 and for the first time we have established them in the uk as well. we will increase this number next year, with 30 new centres, and we will continue our obligation to inform citizens, but that is still not enough. this is not just about information, it is about communication. we have to make it a two-way process. most of our citizens get most of their information from radio and television, so we have to make sure that we help radio and television at all levels to report to citizens on what goes on. that is also part of our policy. we will review regulation (ec) no 1049/2001, because access to information is absolutely crucial. transparency, openness and access to information are central to a new communication policy. of course we discuss the content of policies: that is at the core of everything we do. a communication policy cannot replace good content or good policymaking. that is why we engage in plan d activities, where we invite citizens to participate in the political debate about the future of europe. we take seriously the proposals for practical measures such as agora, which are extremely important. we have analysed the problems with the lack of a real communication policy. we have identified the five areas of action. we want a serious reaction from the european parliament. are these the right areas? if you have other proposals, we would be more than happy to work out very practical ideas, so that we can come back to ask for the necessary budgetary resources. we will combine that with reforming the way we work internally, in order to become more professional, more open, more transparent and more democratic. i thank you for this debate and i hope that we shall continue to discuss these very important principles in trying to establish a communication policy that is right for the european union and all its institutions. in writing. the european globalisation adjustment fund is a one-off charity fund designed to disorient and deceive workers. its aim is supposedly to help and support workers made redundant in a region affected by the relocation of firms, where capital seeks to maximise its profits by moving to countries where the price of labour is lower. the criteria set out in the regulation for its application are so narrow that a minimum number of workers will be eligible, since it is paid in areas where there are at least 1000 redundancies in a single undertaking due to the relocation of undertakings or at least 1000 redundancies in a 6 month period (or 12 months as proposed in the committee's report), representing 1% of employment in the region. it is only requested by the government of a member state and not by the workers or their trade union organisations and is paid by the government only. thus, workers are at the mercy of any government, which can use it selectively as a means of exerting pressure and blackmailing on workers, but also as a means of manipulating consciences and defusing workers' indignation.

in writing. the committee's report on the financing programme for the 'prevention, preparedness and management of the consequences of terrorism' goes even further than the commission's proposal for a decision by adding the protection of vital infrastructure and 'continuous public action' to the objectives of the programme. it is part of the 'reformed eu action programme on terrorism', which focuses on preventing 'violent radicalisation' (!) and protecting the vital infrastructure of the member states and the eu. under this programme, ideological conceptions, positions and attitudes that challenge the "just and sacred" of capitalist barbarity, exploitation and its political systems fall within the concept of "terrorism", while "terrorist acts" can potentially be characterized as conquered and ordinary actions of the mass popular movement, such as symbolic occupations of buildings or streets that can be considered to endanger "vital infrastructure" or the unpredictable functioning of public services. the programmes and measures of european capital and its political representatives against the rights and freedoms of peoples, in the action of popular movements, show exactly their fear. they're not as powerful as they claim. the only time a people is invincible is when they decide to fight back and claim what is rightfully theirs.
in writing. the european return fund is another step in promoting the eu's anti-migration policy. it is part of the broader solidarity and management of migration flows financing programme, which is intended to provide financial support for the 'european fortress', with increased checks and 'rapid reaction forces' at the eu's external borders, a substantial abolition of asylum and refugee protection, and even more repression for economic migrants. the return fund is intended to strengthen the mechanisms for forcible return of 'illegal' migrants to their countries of origin, i.e. it is essentially a fund to facilitate mass deportations of economic migrants and refugees, exposing the hypocritical character of eu declarations on the social integration of migrants. the eu's immigration policy is based solely on the lisbon strategy, with the aim of increasing the profitability of european capital. this policy is shaping the reactionary institutional framework of the member states and the eu, which holds millions of migrants across the eu as illegal or semi-illegal, to hold them hostage to the harshest exploitation of capital with poorly paid, uninsured work, without basic labour rights and excluding them from access to basic social and political rights.

in writing. the proposal for a recommendation reflects the european parliament's fundamental refusal to protect even the minimum of fundamental human rights. after previously voting in favour of the schengen convention, its advanced form, the sis ii information system, while accepting the vis, which legitimizes the collection, processing and exchange of personal data concerning even the political, ideological, philosophical, religious and other views of every eu citizen and the introduction of biometric data and data linked to dna, the political forces of capital now seem to be concerned because the council is heading towards a decision which will not guarantee a 'high level of protection' of personal data. the european parliament, which has already accepted the possibility of transferring personal data to police and intelligence services in third countries, as in the eu-us agreement on the transfer of personal data of europeans travelling by air to the us (pnr), and has agreed to the possibility of transferring personal data even to private individuals (!), now calls on the council to ensure the protection of personal data, but taking into account 'the specific nature of the work of police and judicial authorities'. the hypocritical recommendations of the european parliament cannot hide its full alignment with the policy of legitimizing the surveillance and 'covering' of european citizens.
